author: Stefan Redlich
title: The I-Phonecalypse - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) has seen its market cap getting decimated by more than $250B as lingering concerns about plateauing iPhone sales paired with anecdotal evidence in terms of multiple suppliers cutting guidance and Wall Street weighing in with their own cut in terms of downgrades and slashed price targets ended up in massive selling pressure.
Source: ZdNet - " Here comes the iPhone apocalypse and the end of Apple as we know it " - all IMAGE COURTESY remains
While the rally to $233 was fast and furious and likely at least a tad over-exaggerated, so was the fall down to $175 as fundamentally neither the world is ending for Apple nor has anything changed regarding its long-term appeal.
The "i-phonecalypse" or "i-pocalypse" as I call it is a typical reaction to facts and rumors that have been with Apple for years. While unit sales growth has flattened, this is no reason for concern as Apple considerably raised its ASPs and attracted millions of customers into its ecosystem.
Here are three reasons why that sell-off presents an attractive buying opportunity provided investors are willing and psychologically fit to stick to their purchase amid negative news. But there is also one reason why Apple's strategy could be in the process of backfiring spectacularly.
1) No evidence of supplier cuts being linked to Apple Apple reported another blowout quarter easily beating estimates on the top and bottom line by some magnitude . However, relatively soft guidance for the all-important holiday quarter immediately sent the stock down. During the call, Luca Maestri, Apple's CFO, dropped a bomb when he announced that starting with the December quarter, Apple will stop reporting information on unit sales and ASPs for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. As a result, the stock tanked more than 7% the day after earnings and quickly dropped even below $200 the next week.
Adding to that initial decline were multiple Apple suppliers cutting their guidance as one customer reduced production. The markets interpreted the customer to be Apple. Here is a snapshot of those headlines:
Apple slips after supplier cuts guidance : Lumentum (NASDAQ: LITE ) lowered its Q2 guidance after an unnamed large customer cut 3D sensing orders for the quarter. Apple supplier Qorvo (NASDAQ: QRVO ) cuts Q3 guidance: Qorvo reduced its Q3 guidance from $880M to $900M down to $800M to $840M which is about an 8% cut at the mid-point of both guidance ranges. Another Apple supplier cuts guidance : This time Austrian 3D imaging supplier AMS cuts its guidance citing " recent demand changes from a major consumer customer " by about 15% but did not explicitly name the customer. None of these and other headlines portrayed any proven link to Apple and even if Apple is that ominous major customer Apple's supply chain is so vast, diverse and complex that we as externals have no understanding what it actually means for iPhone sales or demand if a supplier reduces its guidance. It could be that Apple simply ordered more from a different supplier, for instance, Dialog Semiconductor ( OTCPK:DLGNF ) confirmed that they have not seen any drop in demand from Apple or that Apple sees lower demand for lower-priced models which, in turn, would translate into higher ASPs and higher sales offsetting any decline in units.
Also, in the past, we have learnt from Apple directly that more often than not production cuts affect the supply chain more severe than Apple as it is likely that Apple orders more than it reasonably expects to sell in order to ensure it does not run out of stock (due to Apple's giant cash pile they don't have to concentrate as much on working capital as other companies do).
Eventually, trying to extract insights from these guidance cuts is just complete guesswork and nothing a long-term investor should be doing or be worried about.
Instead, such confirmation bias by the markets coupled with Wall Street adding to the pressure in terms of downgrades and price target reductions is always a good indicator to do the opposite.
The most astounding thing about Wall Street, in this case, was actually that they continue to be obsessed with iPhone units and with trimming their own estimates even though they will have no visibility whatsoever on the actuals going forward as Apple will no longer disclose these figures. For instance, Goldman Sachs trimmed iPhone XR and Max unit estimates and increased estimates for the lower-priced iPhones as well as reduced iPhone unit estimates for FY19 by 6%.
2) Focus on Services, not on Units Over the years, analysts have been paying way too much attention to iPhone units while the metrics which really count, namely ASP and overall revenue, were just taken for granted as long as this all-important unit sales figure met expectations.
While revenue for iPhones has set new quarterly records throughout Apple's FY2018, unit sales have been virtually flat and analysts are largely treating this as something bad. While they acknowledge that Apple's supreme pricing power as it remodeled its iPhone line-up towards higher priced models has been extremely successful and profitable, they still continue to be overly obsessed with that unit sales figure.
Apple had to constantly provide color, defend and explain its unit sales actuals and its guidance even though this meant hardly anything to how profitable Apple really is. In the end, the main purpose of a business to shareholders is to generate profits and grow them over time and not try to sell as many units as possible at lower prices, especially in case it can reap more by selling less units at a higher price. And that's why Apple finally decided to stop disclosing iPhone unit sales in its reporting and its guidance. Apple CFO Luca Maestri stressed multiple times that iPhone unit sales are " not necessarily representative of the underlying strength of our [Apple's] business ". The "not necessarily representative" part of the statement was a very polite phrasing as, how I interpret it, what he really means is that "We are producing record profits and all you care are our iPhone unit estimates even though we could sell 15% less units and still grow our bottom line!".
Apple's current iPhone product line-up covers a price range from $449 for the 4.7-inch iPhone 7 via the iPhone 8 Plus starting from $699 to its flag-ship model iPhone XS Max with maximum memory with a price tag of $1,449. That's a range of $1,000 and why should investors pay close attention to unit sales given that it could be a unit representing $500 or one worth almost $1,500. In these cases, using unit sales to judge the underlying strength of Apple's iPhone business is simply misleading.
What's more important is that now that Apple got rid of its unit sales based reporting, it can now focus on what truly matters, namely its evolution from a purely hardware company to a services company. Speaking of Apple's Services division, this fast-growing segment has generated $10B in the last quarter representing around 16% of total sales. Apple remains well on track, in fact, even ahead of its own plan, to double its Services revenue of FY2016 by FY2020, which would represent $48.8B or around $12.2B on average by quarter. Compared to the reported quarter, this represents another 28% growth over the next two years, and given the strong momentum we are seeing right now, I would not be surprised if Apple would even exceed that.
In all five geographic segments, Services revenue grew by strong double-digit year over year. Such broad-based growth set quarterly records for all of Apple's Services components such as Apple Care, Apple Pay, and the AppStore. Tim Cook specifically pointed out the performance at Apple Pay during the earnings call:
Transaction volume tripled year-over-year. And to put that into perspective, Apple Pay generated significantly more transactions than even PayPal Mobile with over 4 times the growth rate.
Source: Apple Earnings Call FY2018/Q4, Tim Cook
The only analyst agreeing with me here and being even more bullish on Services is Morgan Stanley's Katy Huberty. Amid a sea of red in Apple's stock price due to supplier cuts and analyst downgrades, she raised her price target from $226 to $253 explicitly citing Services growth . A survey conducted among smartphone users in U.S. and China signaled greater confidence in a long-term 20% growth trajectory for Services. Although I have no access to her analysis, the key quote from Seeking Alpha already conveys the message:
While the market read announced changes to Apple financial disclosures negatively last week, we view it as a corroborating data point that Apple is approaching a services-led margin inflection, similar to when Amazon began breaking out AWS revenue and profits in 1Q15
That's exactly what all this is about! And now that with the next earnings release, we will finally get more insights into how margins in the Services segment compare with those in the hardware business. We will get a really good read on what sustained 20% Services growth could imply to Apple's profitability. Apple on its own is targeting $48.8B in Services by FY2020 and once we get the GM on that, the market should quickly reevaluate the stock and conclude that Apple's current valuation of only 14 times earnings - and even less if we deduct its net cash position - does not reflect that, especially as Services, which predominantly are subscriptions apart from the individual purchases on the AppStore, should provide a very predictable and reliable stream of income. It may not be viewed as reliable and predictable as let's say food, groceries, and dairies but certainly as more reliable and predictable as a pure hardware business. I truly expect the market to place more appreciation on Apple's Services segment and, in turn, award a higher valuation to the stock. As such, as painful as the more than 20% decline may look in your portfolio, always think long term and instead of panicking, carefully assess whether you have additional funds available you won't need over the next 5-10 years to invest into Apple. In the end, always consider that no matter how sharp and steep the decline in a great company's stock has been, basic market dynamics namely that for every SELLER there is also a BUYER always remain intact.
3) Massive buybacks and dividend growth Although Apple returned almost $90B to shareholders in dividends ($13.7B) and share repurchases ($72.7B), its cash pile is so large that it can return an additional $122.6B before reaching its net cash position of 0. Such massive buybacks have helped reduce the share count by 6.7% over the last year.
AAPL Shares Outstanding data by YCharts
All this will help to propel earnings growth and reduce the multiple (if the stock stays flat) regardless of any top-line growth. Moreover, Apple could even return much more to shareholders in FY2019. Conservatively, assuming Apple's FCF stays at least flat compared to its FY2017 level (FY2018 may have been an exceptionally strong year), it would generate an additional $52B it could allocate to dividends, repurchases, debt repayments etc.
Apple's dividend history is still very young with only 5 consecutive years of dividend growth. However, the company is very committed to shareholders and its dividend policy, and given its supreme operating metrics, I fully expect Apple to become a Dividend Aristocrat by 2037.
Investing in companies substantially growing their dividend over almost decades returns exponentially growing dividend income. Apple is a very likely candidate to achieve that type of growth.
In the past, Dividend Aristocrats have vastly outperformed the broad market , and investing today into companies on their venture towards that illustrious status should return equally market-beating returns.
The key challenge for investors remains to identify those future Aristocrats, and with Apple, I am very confident that by the year 2037, we can welcome the Cupertino-based company to the illustrious Dividend Aristocrat Circle. Yes, Apple will have become a Dividend Aristocrat by 2037 .
And now on to the ugly side... As investors no matter how strong the arguments may be to buy a certain stock, there is always at least one counterargument. Every company faces risks, even for the biggest and richest companies, there are scenarios where dominant market share, above-market margins, or other moats have or could have evaporated. For Apple, the biggest risk I currently see is that despite the anecdotal evidence presented above, these may actually be the first hints that Apple's high-end premium pricing strategy has started to backfire. Could it be that this time, even though that has been said many times before, enormously high prices for the new iPhones despite a feature set lacking any mouthwatering innovation Apple went too far?
Although at this stage, it is just speculation or noise, but it could also contain at least a bit of truth that demand for the new models is (substantially) weaker than expected, especially for the XR, the "cheapest" of the new models. This was meant to be the iPhone to primarily attract more price-conscious customers but a price of EUR 849 is anything but cheap. For a while, customers were willing to pay 4-digit prices, but compared to the X which brought more innovation, the new iPhones are merely faster, wider, and more expensive, not necessarily a good value proposition. Apple's marketing was creative coming up with terms like a "Bionic" chip and a "Super Retina" display, but if that is enough to sell an up to almost $1,500 iPhone is another question. Apple stores are still packed with people no matter where you go and the iPhone as a status symbol is ubiquitous, especially in business, but deteriorating macroeconomic conditions in key emerging countries (BRI) and the tariff risk in China coupled with a potentially less attractive price-to-feature could ultimately end that Apple either loses market share, margin or both. Crossing the 4-digit barrier with the iPhone X sending ASPs soaring worked out like a treat but whether that can continue with even more expensive iPhones is a totally different question. The next quarterly earnings release will probably be the most important one for Apple in recent years as this will tell us just how profitable Apple's Services segment is and whether the doom and gloom surrounding supplier cuts and lower demand following higher pricing is justified.
Investor Take-Away I am very long Apple and even though I am personally not impressed with the feature set of the new iPhone models, this by no means that consumers, in general, think alike. With every investment, there is a valid bull and a valid bear case. However, if you always believe in the bear case, which can always sound very credible and convincing, then by definition no company would ever succeed and prevail.
No matter what happens with the current iPhone generation, I am very confident that Apple will continue to be the most profitable business raking in massive amounts of cash flow and returning it to shareholders. Although for the stock, every new iPhone needs to be a blockbuster, for the company that is certainly not the case as it has more than enough firepower to nail the next one again. I do not give a lot of thought to what is happening in Apple's supply chain or whether Apple cannot grow the number of iPhones it sells. What is more important in the long run is that customers will flock into Apple's ecosystem, stay there and generate predictable and rising income for Apple. And investors not buying the "Services" story should always consider that Apple's R&D spending has been rising continually and sooner or later it will release an entirely new product category. And if that does not work out, it can simply buy into new markets and design a superior product.
The stock's weakness may very well continue and if the next ER shows that the new iPhones are lagging the demand, the stock has a lot of downside potential. Mr. Buffet and Mr. Maestri will sure be ready to pick up on any continued weakness and as regards the latter I hope that Apple is sane enough not to buy back stock too early. If they are already seeing any indications that may derail its guidance, they should simply wait with repurchases as even the biggest pockets are not unlimited.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL.
